newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk coalition digs in under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Turk coalition digs in under pressure.

text.p: Turkey's coalition government on Thursday closed ranks under pressure from leftists and the strongly secularist army, worried by what they fear is the government's resurgent Islamic radicalism.

"As long as our partner complies with the coalition protocol, I do not see that there will be any problems in the government...And given that there are no problems with the protocol, the government will continue with its duties," said Hayri Kozakcioglu, deputy chairman of the True Path Party (DYP).

Two leftist parties have filed censure motions against the government to "safeguard the secular system" and the army put on a show of force this week, parading tanks through an Islamist- held district where an anti-Israeli protest had taken place.
A censure motion effectively means a vote of confidence in the coalition between the Islamist Welfare Party and the True Path.

The partnership has been strained by proposals during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan put forward by Moslem-based Welfare in an apparent attempt to make good some of its pre-election promises to its party grassroots.

The plans include the lifting of a ban on Islamic headscarves for women civil servants, paving the road for overland pilgrimages to the Moslem holy city of Mecca and the construction of mosques in historic secularist strongholds, including the Christian quarter of the former Ottoman capital.
The furore over the proposals and the anti-Israeli rally in Ankara's Sincan district prompted speculation that Turkey was on the brink of its fourth military coup since 1960.
President Suleyman Demirel said in an interview with private TGRT television that the anti-Israeli protest was "unfortunate", but said a military coup would be inappropriate.
"In the end, there is a government here, and this government depends on the confidence vote of the parliament," he said. "It is up to parliament whether it likes (the government) or not."
In a message marking this week's 60th anniversary of secularism entering the constitution, Erbakan reasserted his commitment to the status quo:

"The acceptance of the secular state that marks the turning point in the rise of the Turkish republic on new foundations has enabled the reconciliation of freedom of religion and conscience with a civilised, pluralist political democracy," Erbakan said.

The censure vote must take place within 16-23 days from the time of filing the motion. The outcome is far from certain, with the main opposition conservatives so far loathe to commit themselves to a vote they regard as premature.

The leftist parties have a total of 122 votes against the government's 279 in the 550-seat house. The leftists say some dissident government MPs will support the motion, which needs an absolute majority of 276 to win.
The ruling alliance was boosted on Wednesday by the rejection, by 269 votes to 259, of a new parliamentary corruption probe against deputy prime minister Tansu Ciller.
Ciller formed an alliance with Erbakan in June after corruption allegations piled up against her and Welfare has so far helped quash four attempts to send her to the Supreme Court.
Analysts say the pressure on Welfare has increased their mutual dependence.

"Ciller was saved from...investigation by Welfare's votes. Tansu Ciller's only aim in continuing this government was this. But for the first time in a long time, Ciller has the upper hand," said Ismet Berkan, columnist in the Radikal daily.
"Welfare MPs who are extremely afraid of losing their seats in government, are tightly clinging onto Ciller," he said.
